title: Disney Leaders Talk Streaming Strategy and Growth Drivers: Sports, Local Language, Vertical Media and Emerging Formats
description: Amid a torrent of fan-friendly news about Disney projects across the media spectrum, Disney leadership took time on the first day of the three-day D
body:
Amid a torrent of fan-friendly news about Disney projects across the media spectrum, Disney leadership took time on the first day of the three-day D23 fan fest weekend in Anaheim for panels that offered a behind the scenes look at the Mouse House’s business strategies and vision for driving growth in the streaming era. 

	One of the topics tackled was how to reach next-generation Disney fans with next-generation content formats to keep the company’s many franchises relevant to Gen Alpha and beyond. Disney’s push into the booming vertical media space — aka microdramas and other shortform clips designed to be viewed on mobile phones — was discussed in detail during a session with Eric Schrier, Disney’s president of Direct-to-Consumer International Originals, Strategic Programming and Emerging Media, and Erin Teague, who is executive VP of Product Management for Disney Entertainment and ESPN. 
	

	The conversation was moderated by Jon YouShaei, a YouTube and Instagram executive turned creator and podcaster, and it also featured the perspective of Disney-centric creator Blake Silva as a panelist.


	Schrier emphasized that the “Verts” push on Disney+ is a significant investment for the Mouse. The company last week unveiled a pact with TikTok designed to encourage more fans to create clips with authorized Disney IP. This is a big change for the company that has historically vigorously enforced its copyright and trademark rights.

	“We’ve always looked at making film and television in very finite formats. Half hours, hours, featurelength films. And now you can tell any story. Creators are just storytellers,” Schrier said. “We’ve always talked about our creators before there were actually creators. The creator of ‘Paradise,’ Dan Fogelman, he’s a creator. We talk about them as creators. And so they’re just different types of storytellers. So how do we bring those stories to Disney+? How do we complement what we already have on platform? And it’s early days, but we’re really excited about this next generation of storytellers that are out there that are into Disney+.”
	

	Teague pointed to examples that demonstrate how smart promotion and word-of-mouth via social media helps drive viewership to Disney’s biggest investments in TV and film.



	

					Creator Blake Silva, Disney’s Eric Schrier and Erin Teague and moderator Jon Youshaei speak Aug. 14 at D23: The Ultimate Disney Fan Event in Anaheim. (The Walt Disney Company/Image Group L.A.)
									The Walt Disney Company
	



	“There will never be a replacement for that long-form original content but what is interesting is the way that it is now being supplemented by the shorter form analysis, the clips,” Teague said. As with live game coverage for sports, she said, “the additional commentary and analysis around the game is just as interesting. And so the ways that we can merge those experiences to give people exactly what they want, when they want it in a split second, I think, is the challenge.”

	Silva asserted that most experienced creators who hone their focus on key brands and franchises know how to plug themselves in to the company’s priorities. He said the TikTok deal and Disney+’s embrace of creator content has been invigorating for the Disney-verse.

	“We look at social media and clips going viral, about movies or scenes from movies all the time,” Silva said. “So imagine how that would translate and convert when they’re already in the app, to watchit immediately. I really believe in the creator to talent pipeline. It’s really exciting to think how could this create the next Mister Rogers, my idol.”

	Teague underscored that fans expect to be part of the action in ways that were unimaginable to their parents and grandparents.

	“Next generations of fans are expecting more from their entertainment experience. They want to be a part of the story. They want to put themselves in the story. They want interactivity. They want to have more agency in the storytelling experience with the democratization of creativity,”  Teague said.

	Teague also took part in a session on how ESPN’s increasingly global sports profile is helping Disney find subscribers and fans.

	“ESPN is effectively synonymous with sports as a brand. So diehard sports fans know and love ESPN and have forever, that will never change. We will never stop serving the diehard, loyal sports fan because that’s our base,” Teague said during the session moderated by Joe Earley, Co-President of Direct to Consumer for Disney Entertainment.
	

	“But two trends are happening. One, the internet and native generations. Gen Alpha, Gen Z, etc. They are now expecting more from their sports fandom and their sports experience,” Teague said. “The technology is evolving and we’re thinking about how to also superserve the casual sports fan, because that fandom is equally as real. And it turns out it looks very similar to Disney fandom. And so we’re thinking about this consistently across our product experiences.”

	Freddy Rolón, ESPN’s head of global sports and talent office, reeled off the latest stats for ESPN’s reach with 43 linear networks in more than 130 countries and territories, and it is available on Disney+ in more than 100 markets. For the month of June, ESPN reached 640 million digital and social users.

	“We reach more casual fans, we reach more female fans on Disney+ and then on the flip side, ESPNbrings to Disney+ a credibility about sports, authenticity about sports, and then really a recurring reason for fans to come back to the platform. Not just for the games, but for the game around the game,” Rolón said. “When we think about all those platforms, they work in concert. They’re not necessarily individual. We think about the game on Disney+, the coverage, and the social media platforms all working together to reach fans with information when they want it.”



	

					Disney’s Erin Teague, Freddy Rolón, Jo Fox and Joe Earley speak Aug. 14 at D23: The Ultimate Disney Fan Event in Anaheim. (The Walt Disney Company/Image Group L.A.)
									The Walt Disney Company
	



	Jo Fox, senior VP of marketing for ESPN, said the tighter connection to Disney+ as the platform has expanded significantly across Europe, Middle East, Asia and Latin America has been hugely beneficial. ESPN has made the strategic decision to make key programs available via Disney+ even for subscribers who don’t get the bundle.

	“We use the Disney+ platform and their audience, who might be different to our ESPN core audience, and we can talk to them more directly and get them more enthused about sports and ultimately engaging with Disney+ and ESPN as well,” Fox said. “So as an example of that, we will have select college football games and ‘College GameDay’ unlocked on Disney+ coming up. Because the mascots, the pageantry, the tribal nature of it, the excitement around it. It seems like an amazing sport to be able to unlock some of these select games on Disney+ and talk to this new fan base.”
	

	Earley also moderated a session on Disney+’s international content strategy for local-language production with Schrier and Carol Choi, Disney Asia Pacific’s executive VP of Integrated Marketing & APAC Original Strategy.

	It’s a balancing act of leveraging the platform’s worldwide reach with the need to keep subscribers engaged on a consistent basis. Local-language content has long been seen as key to reducing subscriber churn rates. 

	“What we’re really looking to do is tell stories for local audiences and be hyper-local. We call it local for local. So we make French shows for France, Spanish shows for Spain, or Brazilian shows for Brazil. And we do that all over the world,” Schrier said. “We’re going to be increasing that significantly to have local audiences have something that expresses their culture and their sensibility. And what’s happened organically out of that local for local strategy is that those stories are now traveling back to other parts of the world.”

	Korea and Japan are prime areas of focus for Disney+ and local-language production.

	“Our local creators and storytellers really appreciate the ability for them to tell stories that are authentic to the local cultures with the support of people who’ve been telling stories like their whole career, like Eric and his team,” Choi said. “With that guidance, we’ve been very fortunate to have produced a number of hits, as well as having audiences outside of APAC discover these stories and content.” 

	Choi pointed to recent buzzy Disney+ series including “Tempest,” “Perfect Crown” and “A Shop For Killers.” Earley added, “Some of those Korean dramas put up numbers that rival or even exceed some of the global originals as well.”

	(Pictured top: Disney’s Eric Schrier, Carol Choi and Joe Earley speak at D23 in Anaheim on Aug. 14.)

schema.headline: Disney Leaders Talk Streaming Strategy and Growth Drivers: Sports, Local Language, Vertical Media and Emerging Formats

title: ‘RuPaul’s Drag Race,’ ‘All Stars’ and ‘Untucked’ Renewed for New Seasons at MTV and Paramount+
description:
Shantay you stay! 

	“RuPaul’s Drag Race,” “All Stars” and “Untucked” have all been renewed for new seasons at MTV and Paramount+.

	The franchise’s
body:
Shantay you stay! 

	“RuPaul’s Drag Race,” “All Stars” and “Untucked” have all been renewed for new seasons at MTV and Paramount+.

	The franchise’s main show, “RuPaul’s Drag Race” will return to MTV for its 19th season. This follows a successful season 18 which delivered double-digit growth over the previous season and set a new franchise premiere viewership record. The series was up 19% on P18-49 rating (0.564 vs. 0.472) and up 7% in P18-49 share (2.43 vs. 2.27). Season 18 of “Drag Race” ranked among the Top 3 cable series in 2026 to date in the key demo.
	

	 Season 18 featured iconic guest judges including Cardi B, Teyana Taylor, Benny Blanco and more. Myki Meeks took home the crown.


	“RuPaul’s Drag Race: Untucked,” the aftershow, will also return for season 18.

	The show’s production company, World of Wonder said, “Nearly twenty years later, what began as a dream has become an extraordinary global movement. We owe endless thanks to our partners at MTV and Paramount+, along with every queen, judge, crew member, and fan who has built ‘RuPaul’s Drag Race.’ Drag brings people together in powerful ways –  and we are honored to keep celebrating new voices and sharing iconic moments with the world.”

	Paramount+ has also renewed “RuPaul’s Drag Race All Stars” for season 12 following the return of its Tournament of All Stars format, which brought together returning queens to compete for a coveted spot in the “Drag Race Hall of Fame.” Crystal Methyd earned the title during the latest season. The season also featured the franchise’s first all-disco Lip Sync Smackdown for the Crown and welcomed guest judges Kate Hudson, La Toya Jackson, Reneé Rapp and others to the panel. ‘RuPaul’s Drag Race All Stars: Untucked’ will also return for season 9.
	

	As Emmy voting gets underway, the show landed 11 nominations, including an outstanding host for a reality or reality competition program nod for RuPaul. The nomination was historic and was a record-extending 11th consecutive nomination.

title: ‘The State of Us’ Review: A Pair of Spirited Performances Lift a Familiar Yorkshire Tearjerker
description: The weather being what it is in Yorkshire, a sunroof is not a top priority for most car buyers in that English county — but the tired hatchback driv
body:
The weather being what it is in Yorkshire, a sunroof is not a top priority for most car buyers in that English county — but the tired hatchback driven by young slacker Frankie (Samuel Bottomley) has one. That’s the first of a few improbabilities in “The State of Us,” an occasionally hokey but winningly sweet-natured buddy comedy from British newcomer Ollie Gardner and Jake Harvey, and it’s a forgivable one: How else, at a key emotional juncture, will his ailing best friend Taylor (Callum Scott Howells) stand up in the car to freely embrace the cold night with arms outstretched? It’s a shameless cliché of an image, recycled from the likes of “The Perks of Being a Wallflower” and TV’s “Euphoria,” but the film gets away with the steal, in large part because Frankie and Taylor are, at least for a moment, chasing the life they’ve seen in slicker American youth movies.
	

	The life they actually live, meanwhile, mixes grainily downbeat British social realism of the Paul Laverty-scripted Ken Loach school with flashes of more Hollywoodized sentimentality and narrative contrivance — as Taylor, a terminally cancer-stricken young man living in a hospice, is broken out of his glum surroundings by Frankie, his irresponsible bestie, cuing one wild night of boyish misbehavior and more mature emotional reckonings. 


	The result isn’t always convincing, but it’s far more consistently likable, thanks in large part to lively performances by Howells (TV’s “It’s a Sin”) and especially Bottomley (“How to Have Sex”), who maintain a key sense of hard-times kinship and tension in the bond at the film’s center. Premiering in the main competition at Edinburgh, “The State of Us” should continue to please crowds at smaller festivals; theatrical prospects are modest, but streaming and broadcast potential is strong.
	

	A brief prologue outlines the childhood damage still borne by boisterous ne’er-do-well Frankie, who lost his mother at an early age, and whose incapable father left him to be raised in Taylor’s more stable household; already best buds, the boys wound up closer to brothers. When we cut to the present day, however, it’s clear something unspecified has gone awry in this chosen-family setup. The friends haven’t seen each other in some time, though Frankie spends many an evening parked outside the hospice in his car, summoning the gumption to visit. When he does, it’s after hours: Breaking into the building via an elderly patient’s window, he ropes a bewildered Taylor into his late-night escape plan without so much as a friendly catch-up. 

	His rashness may be ill-advised, but it does abet the film’s fleet pacing: Cut to a brisk 90 minutes by ace editor Chris Gill (“Kneecap,” “28 Days Later”) and Abi Wright, “The State of Us” ably swings between tragedy and farce in the course of its overnight structure, even making more-or-less sense of an awkwardly shoehorned romantic subplot between Taylor and enigmatic cool girl Rosie (Safia Oakley-Green, the gifted star of indie horror “Out of Darkness,” making the most of a stock role), whom he meets at the scuzzy house party Frankie insists on crashing, and with whom he has more in common than meets the eye. 

	The extended party setpiece allows for some amusing scatological hijinks, but the film is most moving and enjoyable when simply focused on its two leads, whether talking things out in the car or on the country hill of sundry childhood memories. (“The Outrun” DP Yunus Roy Imer keeps the shooting intimate and unfussy, but the rolling beauty of the Yorkshire landscape offers some valuable background support.) Howells, gifted the more openly sympathetic role, puts his naturally anxious brows and forlorn demeanor to good use as Taylor, without making him too much of a victim; there are glimpses here of the buoyant, nurturing partner that he used to be in the friendship. 

	But it’s Bottomley who impresses most here, at every turn lining Frankie’s obnoxious, juvenile antics with soulful self-doubt, and terror of yet more grief crashing his still-young life. As “The State of Us” unsubtly but effectively turns on the waterworks, it’s him, as much as his dying friend, we find ourselves dabbing our eyes for. He, too, has earned some time out of the sunroof.

schema.headline: ‘The State of Us’ Review: A Pair of Spirited Performances Lift a Familiar Yorkshire Tearjerker

title: Selena Gomez Slams ‘Completely Meritless’ Wondermind Lawsuit, Will File to Dismiss ‘Baseless Claims’
description: Selena Gomez and her legal team have released a fiery statement after the “Only Murders in the Building” star was accused of defrauding investors in
body:
Selena Gomez and her legal team have released a fiery statement after the “Only Murders in the Building” star was accused of defrauding investors in her mental health startup, Wondermind, in a federal lawsuit filed Thursday. 

	“The allegations that Selena Gomez engaged in any way whatsoever in any purported ‘fraud’ or other wrongdoing are completely meritless, both factually and legally,” Gomez’s litigator, Mathew S. Rosengart, told People. “We will vigorously defend these false allegations and indeed are filing a motion to dismiss the baseless claims against her.”
	

	According to The New York Times, the lawsuit, which also names Gomez’s mother and Wondermind co-founder Mandy Teefey as a defendant, claims the Wondermind team “falsely represented” the trajectory and leadership structure of the media company, which was founded in 2021 as a way to make mental health resources more accessible. Investors claimed that Gomez and her mother solicited about $1.2 million from them.


	The suit alleges that Gomez had signed a contract stating that she would be “actively building the company as its head of marketing,” but has since “ignored” the agreement. It also claims that there were said to be partnerships with Fidelity and J.P. Morgan that would allow Wondermind to provide mental health services to their employees, but they “did not exist.” Celebrity profiles, a “groundbreaking app” and advertising deals that were promised also fell through, the lawsuit states.

	The lawsuit also says that Wondermind “quietly collapsed around them,” while “not one of its founders, officers, or directors said a word to the investors.” Investors claim they only found out about the “utter financial and operational disarray at Wondermind” from a 2025 story published by The Cut. The exposé alleged that Gomez was trying to distance herself from the company and outlined the messy firing of chief executive Daniella Pierson.
	

	Teefey has yet to comment on the suit, but Pierson told The New York Times that she “categorically denies the allegations against her and welcomes the opportunity to present concrete documentation and financial records that establish the facts.”

schema.headline: Selena Gomez Slams ‘Completely Meritless’ Wondermind Lawsuit, Will File to Dismiss ‘Baseless Claims’

title: Slipknot Confirms Sid Wilson’s Sudden Exit: ‘We Wish Him the Best’
description:
Slipknot is officially parting ways with Sid Wilson, who had been part of the group for nearly 30 years.

	“Effective immediately, Slipknot will no
body:
Slipknot is officially parting ways with Sid Wilson, who had been part of the group for nearly 30 years.

	“Effective immediately, Slipknot will no longer be associated with Sid Wilson,” the band posted on its Instagram account in a post that has since been taken down. “We wish him the best in his future endeavors.”

	The DJ and keyboardist had been part of the heavy metal group since 1998, a year before Slipknot’s first studio album was released.
	

	News of Wilson’s departure was first reported by TMZ in late July, although the reason that Slipknot decided to kick him out remains unclear. That same day, Slipknot guitarist Jim Root posted a message on his Instagram story set to the band’s 2008 song “‘Til We Die.”


	“Don’t believe everything you read,” Root wrote. “Stop. Think. Take a breath. Sit with it for awhile. Maybe. Just maybe even wait until there’s more information.”

	Wilson’s exit comes after Craig Jones left the band in 2023 and Chris Fehn left in 2019. Joey Jordison died in 2021, while Paul Gray died in 2020. Slipknot’s albums include “Slipknot,” “Iowa,” “Vol. 3,” “All Hope Is Gone,” “.5: The Gray Chapter,” “We Are Not Your Kind” and “The End, So Far,” which was released in 2022.

	The band’s most recent live performance was in July 2025 at Inkcarceration, a music and tattoo festival in Ohio.

	The remaining members of Slipknot have yet to speak out about Wilson’s sudden departure and what it means for the future of the band.

schema.headline: Slipknot Confirms Sid Wilson’s Sudden Exit: ‘We Wish Him the Best’

title: ‘Lanterns’ Bosses and Stars on How the Show’s Grounded Approach Ushers in an ‘Entirely Different Kind of Superhero’
description: As part of James Gunn and Peter Safran’s newly expanded DCU, a more grounded take on the “Green Lantern” comics may surprise audiences who associate
body:
As part of James Gunn and Peter Safran’s newly expanded DCU, a more grounded take on the “Green Lantern” comics may surprise audiences who associate the character with the Ryan Reynolds film that received poor reviews back in 2011.

	But for co-creators Chris Mundy, Damon Lindelof and Tom King, “Lanterns” is all about going back to the original iteration of the character when he was “an entirely different kind of superhero.”


	“We’re talking about almost a century’s worth of storytelling, and now we get to carry that baton,” Lindelof told Variety. “But then at the same time, the audience is hungry for something original and relevant, and they want storytellers to take risks. Those risks can’t feel like they’re gimmicks; they have to feel like they have real emotional stakes.”
	

	The show follows Hal Jordan (Kyle Chandler) as he is forced to take John Stewart (Aaron Pierre) under his wing as a backup. As the Green Lantern, Hal has the power to create material items through his ring and acts as an intergalactic space officer. Things take a dark turn after a series of unexplainable deaths draw Hal and John to a small town in Nebraska.

	As creators, King brings a wealth of experience as a comic book writer, while Lindelof created the “Watchmen” TV series. Mundy, who served as showrunner on “Ozark,” is new to the comic book world.

	“I know that if Damon didn’t work on this show, I would have used — and I think Tom would say the same — ‘Watchmen’ as a real touchstone of how you do a show and have it be emotional and about real people, while also honoring the comic book part of it,” Mundy said.
	

	In addition to the grounded approach that “Watchmen” takes, “Lanterns” also shares similarities in how the show explores race, colonization and justice. King explained how “there’s a wonderful coincidental parallel with comics that ‘Watchmen,’ in the ’80s, set the standard for a generation of comic book writers who were like, ‘Oh, we can talk about those themes using superheroes!'”

	Poorna Jagannathan, who plays the conniving and mysterious Zoe, hopes that shows like “Lanterns” invite more actors into the DCU who don’t read comic books.

	“I thought I’d be with a green screen wearing a suit, talking to no one at all, just into the abyss,” she told Variety at Thursday’s premiere on the Paramount lot. “I hesitated because I didn’t know this world at all. I felt like I didn’t belong, actually. I felt bad that I was so ignorant about it.”

	“I don’t think that only this universe will be affected by it; I think every show in the genre will be affected by what happened on ‘Lanterns,'” she added. “It’ll be a blueprint on how to take something big and keep it with a beating heart.”

	As the DCU continues to expand and test the waters of audiences, both with the success of films like “Superman” and the underwhelming reception to “Supergirl,” how audiences react to “Lanterns” could determine if early conversations about Season 2 turn into an official renewal.

	“The one thing that fans hate more than being listened to is fan service and that sort of idea of doing something just to placate them. And so I do think that fandom is not a monolith,” Lindelof said of navigating fandom expectations. “There are some fans who want more risky, edgy sort of revisionist storytelling inside of these adaptations, and some fans who are just basically like, ‘Give me what I love.'”

	There are certain canonical elements that the “Lanterns” team had to carefully maneuver, such as how the show ties into John Stewart’s involvement in “Man of Tomorrow,” and the return of Guy Gardner (Nathan Fillion), who also appears in “Superman” and “Peacemaker.”

	But when it comes to what “Lanterns” might signal for the future of the newly revamped DCU, it’s all about creative voices being at the forefront.

	“You can’t go out of bounds in terms of storylines that James and Peter want to do,” Lindelof said. “But artistically, they’re giving us a lot of freedom to tell the story how we want.”
	

	“Lanterns” premieres Sunday, Aug. 16 on HBO Max.

schema.headline: ‘Lanterns’ Bosses and Stars on How the Show’s Grounded Approach Ushers in an ‘Entirely Different Kind of Superhero’

title: ‘How the F— Would You Get This Movie Made in America?’ Christine Vachon, Film4, BBC Film Put ‘Trainspotting,’ ‘Ratcatcher’ and ‘The Wicker Man’ Through the 2026 Greenlight Test
description: Would “Trainspotting” get financed today? Could Lynne Ramsay survive the jump from shorts to a first feature? And might “The Wicker Man,” once treat
body:
Would “Trainspotting” get financed today? Could Lynne Ramsay survive the jump from shorts to a first feature? And might “The Wicker Man,” once treated as a problem child, now look like exactly the kind of genre package buyers chase?

	That was the conceit of a lively session hosted by Wendy Mitchell, with Picturehouse’s creative director Clare Binns, Killer Films’ Christine Vachon, Film4’s head of distribution and sales Stefanie Fahrion, BBC Film’s commissioning executive Alice Ojha and Casarotto’s Simon Renshaw asked to assess British classics as if they had just landed on their desks in 2026.
	

	Nobody suggested the market had become kinder, but several films looked less risky than their loglines might suggest.

	
		The Talking Factor	

	First up was “Trainspotting”: heroin use, a dead baby, filthy toilets, heavy Scottish dialect and no obvious box-office cast.

	Binns immediately went to Danny Boyle’s previous film, calling “Shallow Grave” “one of the most exciting films I ever saw” and saying it announced “a new voice.” Fahrion saw upside in the extremity. The film had “so many iconic moments,” she said, with enough “shock value” to create a “talking factor” and “FOMO” around scenes audiences felt they had to see, and today would likely virally share. Renshaw called it “a big swing,” but also “something that’s going to get people talking.” Vachon was less concerned still. “I pitch it as genre or genre adjacent,” she said. At the right price, “I don’t think it’s risky at all.”
	
		Soft Money, Then Sell	

	Structure was the focus for Bill Forsyth’s feel good “Local Hero.” “I don’t think you get any American equity or a pre-buy unless it was a really big, big star,” said Vachon. Better, she argued, to make it “with as much soft money as possible” and then sell it for “a nice high price to the U.S.”
	

	Binns saw an audience play. Older cinemagoers remain underserved, she said. “They might not come opening weekend,” but “this will be a word of mouth” film.
	
		First Features: Still the Hurdle	

	Ramsay’s “Ratcatcher” brought the financing gap into sharper focus.

	Renshaw called “that leap from shorts to that first feature” the hurdle, with known cast often crucial in getting financiers and distributors comfortable.

	This is where, in the U.K. at least, public backing can enter. Fahrion noted that voices as unique and challenging as Ramsay’s often originate with public development or production money.

	Vachon’s U.S. take was starker. “What is this public funding of which you speak?” she joked, before proposing another panel title: “How the fuck would you get this movie made in America?”

	Her answer: “We’d make it for about $300,000.” The job, she said, is to ask: “How do we create a case for this?”
	
		Genre Looks Safer	

	Then came “The Wicker Man”: paganism, full frontal nudity, a remote island and human sacrifice.

	Vachon called it “exactly what… the A24s, Neons, etc. are looking for right now.” Renshaw noted it could be made inexpensively, while Binns saw a hook in casting an actor, in that classics case Richard Chamberlain, “doing something new, different for him.” 

	How times change: when released British Lion packaged it as the secondary feature to “Don’t Look Now.” 

	And the worst pitch Renshaw ever received?

	“’The Sixth Sense,’ but it’s a dog.”

schema.headline: ‘How the F— Would You Get This Movie Made in America?’ Christine Vachon, Film4, BBC Film Put ‘Trainspotting,’ ‘Ratcatcher’ and ‘The Wicker Man’ Through the 2026 Greenlight Test

title: Director Frieda Luk on Olivia Luccardi’s ‘Sacred Creatures’ Role and the Fine Line Between ‘Crazy’ and ‘Enlightened’
description:
For “Sacred Creatures” director Frieda Luk, belief can be comforting, ridiculous, exhilarating and hard to explain.

	“I’m really fascinated by when
body:
For “Sacred Creatures” director Frieda Luk, belief can be comforting, ridiculous, exhilarating and hard to explain.

	“I’m really fascinated by when people believe in something,” she tells Variety. “One person believes in something, and then a group of people, and then it slowly becomes this massive phenomenon. It goes viral.”

	That fascination drives Luk’s debut feature, which world premieres in competition at the Edinburgh International Film Festival. Starring Olivia Luccardi, James Cusati-Moyer and Romina D’Ugo, the Canada-Italy production follows three estranged siblings reuniting in rural Italy after middle sister Miriam (Olivia Luccardi) is released from psychiatric treatment following an experience she understands as a spiritual awakening rather than a breakdown.
	

	“This movie is my exploration of believing in something and belief,” says Luk. “Miriam has agency. She knows herself and she makes choices. However, when she becomes a figure that people rally around, people are imbuing her with meaning. When she becomes abstract, she no longer controls the message.”


	That uncertainty extends to the film itself, which slips between psychological drama, comedy and magical realism without settling comfortably into any of them. For Luk, the tonal slipperiness developed naturally from writing. “I set up the situation and these characters, and as I’m writing, I’m following what they’re doing. What I’m waiting for is how they surprise me,” she says.



	

					Courtesy of Nicolás Villegas
	



	One influence was Marco Ferreri’s “La Grande Bouffe,” the grotesque story of four men attempting to eat themselves to death. “The comedy is following through that premise in a serious way, because if you actually are going to eat yourself to death, you’re going to have gastrointestinal problems,” Luk says. “It’s also very silly. It never takes itself too seriously.” Italian cinema was integral to “Sacred Creatures” from the start. Luk points to films of the 1970s, admiring their willingness to move between modes contemporary cinema can sometimes keep separate. “A lot of the ’70s movies, especially European ones, are completely in between genres.”Luccardi was similarly keen to avoid reducing Miriam to a diagnosis. “She is healing from the lack of belief from people and everyone thinking that something was wrong with her,” Luccardi explains, adding that Miriam feels “meant for something greater.”There was another, less metaphysical piece of direction that unlocked the character: Luk told her Miriam was like a cat.
	

	“She’s very much like: ‘I’m letting you in on my terms. No, I actually don’t want you to touch me. I want to be a pet, but not like that,’” laughs Luccardi.

	“I did a lot of cat direction,” Luk dryly admits.

	As Miriam grows more secure in herself, Luccardi subtly changed the physical quality of the performance.

	“There was more of a calmness in my breath,” she says. “She was more relaxed and calm and just flowed. Before, she may have been a little more stressed and tightly wound.”

	That growing self-possession becomes visual in the film’s party scene, where Miriam arrives in a voluminous yellow-green dress that immediately separates her from the room around her. There is something of Bette Davis’ party entrance in “All About Eve” to the moment: costume becomes a declaration of presence, allowing Miriam to suddenly occupy a different plane from everyone watching her.

	Luk wanted the dress to be “kind of ridiculous looking, but also kind of chic,” something that would “take up some space” without seeming entirely out of place. “Miriam is new and a little ridiculous,” she says, with its uncontained “fluffiness” signalling “an irreverence to what has come before.”

	Luccardi’s relationship with it was rather less reverential by the end of the shoot. “At the beginning, it was great. At the end… I wore it a long time,” she jokes. “As with every costume, you love it at the beginning and then you’re like: ‘Can we burn it, please?’”



	

					Courtesy of Nicolás Villegas
	



	The surrounding family remain skeptical of their sister’s burgeoning allure to those around her. Luk, an only child who grew up surrounded by cousins, was amused by the way relatives can inhabit incompatible versions of the same history.

	“They’re always competing,” she says.

	The instinct of creating a story that makes life easier to comprehend ultimately expands beyond the siblings.Luk grew up without religion, but many childhood friends were religious and invited her to churches and youth groups. Watching from the outside, she was intrigued by their ability to surrender themselves to faith.

	“I would watch them read a text and believe in that text and treat it like this holy thing,” she recalls. “It was really hard for me to give myself over to something like that.”At Catholic services, she found herself captivated by the incense, clothing and ceremony.

	“I was like: ‘This is so fun and theatrical.’ I can see how it could be really comforting,” she says. “There’s a community-oriented spirit to it. Being a fan of a big sport is kind of fun. Yelling at a team is fun.”The director began thinking about fandoms, sports and social media with much the same curiosity. What separates a few people who regularly gather from a movement?
	

	“What if people hung out, and then that becomes a movement?” she says. “A few people hang out, and then more people hang out. Then you do it regularly, and what happens?”

	The film is shot in Piedmont and Italy provided a fertile landscape for those questions. Luk recalls seeing reports about a teenage protester and wondering why there couldn’t be a patron saint for protest, and what the origin story of a new saint might look like.

	But after all that construction of a film, a family history, a faith and perhaps even a saint, the director isn’t interested in providing audiences with a final answer about Miriam.

	“I want people to come away examining why they believe in something and how,” she says, “and that there is a pleasure in believing something.”

	“You never know if you are right or you are wrong. You might be wrong.”

	Or, as Luccardi puts it: “You never know if someone’s crazy or if someone’s enlightened. Who knows?”

	“It’s a fine line.”

schema.headline: Director Frieda Luk on Olivia Luccardi’s ‘Sacred Creatures’ Role and the Fine Line Between ‘Crazy’ and ‘Enlightened’

title: Cambridge Professor's Friend Says He Was Scared to Leave House Hours Before Death
description:
Ex-Cambridge Professor
                          Told Friend in Last Convo He Feared Leaving Hous
body:
Ex-Cambridge Professor
                          Told Friend in Last Convo He Feared Leaving House ...
                          Just Hours Before He Died
                      
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Jason Arday -- the former Cambridge professor accused of plagiarism who was found dead in London Friday -- feared leaving the house amid the media scrutiny just before he died ... according to a longtime friend.
      
    
            Simon Baron-Cohen, the director of the Autism Research Center at the University of Cambridge, appeared on BBC Radio 4's "Today" Saturday ... and he discussed his last conversation with Arday, which he says took place hours before he passed.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Baron-Cohen says Arday confided in him that he was afraid to leave home ... because he felt "bombarded" by the media calling him a fraud.
      

            Baron-Cohen calls Arday "an incredibly kind and gentle and caring and generous man" ... but adds he wasn't coping well with the negative attention. He says Arday's final voice note was about how "he couldn’t go on."
      
    
            Baron-Cohen adds, "We need to let the investigations proceed. We need to understand how this tragedy has happened, but there has to be accountability at lots of levels.”
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            As we reported ... Deborah Prentice, the Vice-Chancellor Professor at the University of Cambridge, confirmed Arday's death Friday, saying, "We are desperately saddened to hear this tragic news" and "our heartfelt sympathies go to Jason Arday’s family and friends at this incredibly difficult time."
      
    
            Cops have not made a determination about his cause of death yet ... but say it appears "unexpected" but not suspicious.
      
    
            Arday was hired by Cambridge in 2023 ... but recently, he's faced a series of plagiarism accusations related to his work for the university. Cambridge launched an investigation into Arday, and he later resigned.
      
    
            He was just 41 years old.
